content: Clinical confirmation of rabies cases should involve the demonstration of viral antigens, antibodies, and nucleic acid amplification products. Each country must have at least one national reference laboratory capable of diagnosing rabies using currently recommended techniques. These laboratories should collaborate with reference centers of the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Standardized case definitions for rabies should be adopted by all countries, supported by laboratory-based surveillance of suspected cases in humans and animals. Rabies typically presents as encephalitis, characterized by hyperactivity (furious rabies) or paralytic syndromes (paralytic rabies), progressing to coma and death within 7–10 days if intensive care is not provided. Death usually results from cardiac or respiratory failure. Rabies cases are classified as follows: Suspected: A case compatible with a clinical case definition. Probable: A suspected case with a reliable history of contact with a suspected, probable, or confirmed rabid animal. Confirmed: A suspected or probable case confirmed through laboratory testing. A presumptive diagnosis of rabies is more straightforward when an individual presents with a compatible illness and documented exposure to a laboratory-confirmed rabid animal. Clinical signs such as hydrophobia, aerophobia, agitation, confusion, and autonomic dysfunction may alternate with periods of lucidity. Spasms, particularly inspiratory spasms, may occur and aid in clinical diagnosis. Paralytic rabies may present with less evident excitation and phobic spasms in only 50% of cases. Early signs of paralytic rabies can include myoedema, piloerection, and fasciculations. However, diagnosing rabies based solely on clinical grounds can be challenging and unreliable, especially in the absence of a history of exposure or typical symptoms. Atypical rabies presentations, such as Guillain-Barré-like syndromes or other unusual features, have been reported, particularly in cases associated with bat or wildlife exposure. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be helpful in such cases, showing abnormalities in the brainstem, hippocampus, hypothalamus, and other regions. Gadolinium enhancement may become apparent in later stages when the patient is comatose. These imaging patterns can help differentiate rabies from other viral encephalitides. Rabies should be included in the differential diagnosis of all patients presenting with unexplained, acute, progressive viral encephalitis, even in areas where the disease is rare. Imported cases and local transmission from wildlife (e.g., bats, foxes, jackals) remain possible. Solid organ transplant recipients presenting with compatible encephalitis should be screened for rabies to prevent transmission. Rabies has the highest case fatality rate of any known infectious disease, necessitating strict biosafety measures when handling lyssaviruses. Biosafety level 2 practices are generally sufficient for routine laboratory activities, but additional precautions, such as personal protective equipment and pre-exposure rabies vaccination, are essential. For ante-mortem diagnosis in humans, samples such as saliva, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), tears, and skin biopsies (including hair follicles from the nape of the neck) can be used. Saliva and skin biopsies provide the highest diagnostic sensitivity. Post-mortem diagnosis relies on brain tissue, which is the preferred specimen. In cases where brain removal is not feasible, less invasive techniques, such as sampling through the foramen magnum or orbital route, can be employed. Diagnostic specimens should ideally be refrigerated or frozen until testing. If this is not possible, preservation in a 50% glycerine-saline solution at ambient temperature is an alternative, though freezing in glycerine is not recommended. Formalin-fixed brain tissue can be used for immunohistochemical methods but is not suitable for routine diagnosis due to delayed results and lower sensitivity compared to other methods. The fluorescent antibody test (FAT) remains the gold standard for rabies diagnosis, relying on the detection of viral antigens in brain tissue. Other methods, such as enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) and the direct rapid immunohistochemistry test (DRIT), have shown comparable sensitivity and specificity to FAT. DRIT is particularly useful for decentralized surveillance and field conditions. Lateral flow tests for rapid antigen detection under field conditions show promise but require further validation. Participation in routine quality management programs is strongly recommended for laboratories performing rabies diagnostic techniques.
